knowledge_type_note: A unit of measurement, not a principle. It is what initiative is counted in.

history.notes: Ordinary chess vocabulary of long standing; no coinage researched or claimed.

engine_era_note: Engines handle time implicitly through search rather than as a term, and they are notably less impressed by tempo-counting than opening books are — a 'lost tempo' that produces a better structure is often simply the right move.

preconditions: A move is being assessed for what it costs or gains in time
indicators_for: The move develops or improves a piece AND forces a reply
The opponent's forced reply does nothing for them
A piece is being moved twice in the opening without compensation — a lost tempo
indicators_against: The 'threat' forcing the reply is not real, so no tempo is gained
The forced reply actually improves the opponent's position — a common trap
The position is closed, where time matters little
false_positive_traps: Chasing a piece with a threat it WANTED to answer is not gaining a tempo — the classic case is driving a piece to a better square with an attack.
Counting tempi in a closed position, where they may be worth nothing.
Treating 'moved the same piece twice' as automatically a lost tempo. This is a registered false-positive case: a capture, an escape, or a decisively better square all justify it.

typical_plans: Develop with threats so each move does two jobs
In the endgame, keep a spare pawn move in reserve as a tempo
Triangulate to lose a tempo deliberately
typical_moves: A developing move that attacks something
A spare pawn move held back in a pawn ending
strategic_consequences: Accumulated tempi become a lead in development and then the initiative

exceptions: 'Losing a tempo' is a virtue in the endgame, where triangulation aims at exactly that.
A tempo has no fixed value; the three-tempi-per-pawn heuristic is an opening rule of thumb only.
Moving the same piece twice is not automatically a lost tempo.
limitations: Not mechanically detectable. Whether a move 'gains a tempo' depends on whether the threat is real and whether the reply helps the opponent.
misconceptions: That a tempo is worth a third of a pawn. It has no fixed value.
That gaining tempi is always good — driving an enemy piece to a better square costs you more than it gains.
That tempo and initiative are the same thing.

by_level.beginner: A tempo is one move's worth of time. You gain one when your move improves your position and forces them to answer with a move that does nothing for them.
by_level.intermediate: A tempo. Check the threat is real and that answering it does not actually help them — that is where tempo-counting usually goes wrong.
by_level.advanced: One unit of time. Note the sign flips in the endgame: losing a tempo by triangulation is the goal there, not a cost.
by_level.master: Tempi are only meaningful relative to the position's sharpness. In a locked structure they are close to worthless; in an open one a single move decides.

by_depth.normal: A tempo is one move considered as time. Gaining one means your move improves your position while forcing a reply that does not improve theirs — the move has to do two jobs.
by_depth.deep: The unit initiative is counted in. Gaining a tempo requires a move that both improves your position and compels a reply that does nothing for the opponent; the common error is 'gaining' a tempo by driving an enemy piece somewhere it preferred to be. The word is also used with the opposite sign in the endgame, where triangulation is described as losing a move on purpose in order to return the same position with the opponent to play. There is no fixed exchange rate with material: the familiar three-tempi-per-pawn figure is an opening heuristic, and in a closed position tempi may be worth nothing at all.

explanations.lesson: A move gains a tempo only if the reply it forces is one your opponent did not want to make. Check that before congratulating yourself.

avoid: a tempo is worth a third of a pawn

definition_short: One move, considered as a unit of time. To 'gain a tempo' is to improve your position while forcing a reply that does not.
definition_long:
A single move regarded as a unit of time. Gaining a tempo means making a move that does two jobs at once — it improves your position AND compels a reply that does not improve theirs. Losing a tempo means spending a move that achieves nothing, or moving the same piece twice for no gain.

The relationship to INITIATIVE is the thing to keep straight, and the two are constantly conflated: a tempo is one unit, the initiative is the sustained state built out of them. Tempi are the coins; the initiative is what you have when you keep spending them profitably.

Confusingly, 'losing a tempo' is also used APPROVINGLY in the endgame, where triangulation is described as losing a move on purpose in order to hand the same position back with the opponent to play. The two usages are opposite in sign and both are standard.

A tempo has NO fixed value. The common rule of thumb that three tempi are worth a pawn is a rough opening heuristic and nothing more: in a sharp position one move decides the game, and in a locked position several are worth nothing at all.
